# Compact Fusion Reactor
The station runs on a compact fusion reactor. The reactor itself makes no electricity: it heats gas. The [color=orange]gas turbine[/color] is a heat engine: it lets heat flow from that hot gas into cold gas and turns part of it into power for the [color=orange]HV network[/color]. Like any heat engine, it needs both a hot side and a cold side.
## Two loops [bold]Hot loop[/bold] (closed): [color=orange]reactor outlet[/color] → turbine [color=orange]hot inlet[/color] → turbine hot outlet → [color=lightblue]reactor inlet[/color]
[bold]Cold loop[/bold] (closed, built by atmospherics): turbine [color=lightblue]cold outlet[/color] → [color=cyan]radiators in space[/color] (and/or coolers) → turbine [color=lightblue]cold inlet[/color]
Examine the reactor and the turbine to see which side each port is on. The reactor and both sides of the turbine move gas on their own; no extra pumps are needed in either loop.
## Where the power comes from - The share of the heat that becomes electricity grows with the temperature difference: [bold]efficiency = 70% × (1 − T cold / T hot)[/bold]. A cold side at 300 K and a hot side at 1500 K give 56%. - Every watt the reactor makes has to leave through the cold loop: as electricity, or as heat dumped by the radiators. [bold]The cold loop decides how hard you can run the reactor.[/bold] - Without cold gas, or with a cold loop that has warmed up, the turbine makes nothing, the hot loop has nowhere to put its heat and the reactor core overheats.
## Filling the loops - Fill both loops to roughly [color=orange]3000–4500 kPa[/color]. Low pressure in the hot loop means the core runs much hotter for the same power. - Nitrogen works. Carbon dioxide, water vapour and nitrous oxide carry a little more heat per mole, frezon far more. Tritium is a poor coolant. - Radiators shed heat much faster when hot, so a cold loop at a few hundred kelvin is normal. Coolers (freezers) help but use power.
Rough numbers for nitrogen at about 4500 kPa: with [bold]~20 radiators[/bold] the reactor can run at about half power and the turbine gives roughly [bold]450–500 kW[/bold]. Full power needs a much larger cold loop (several dozen radiators). Watch the core temperature and raise the power only as far as your cooling allows.
The reactor window and the turbine show pressures, temperatures and flow (mol/s). The turbine tells you when an outlet is full, when no gas flows, or when the cold side is too warm.
## Running the reactor - The containment field needs [color=orange]APC power[/color]. Without it the reactor winds down and the field weakens. - Insert a [color=cyan]fuel cassette[/color]. Cassettes are ordered from cargo. The cassette is locked in while the reactor runs. - The reactor needs power before the turbine makes any: start it from the SMES or batteries. - Set the power and press [bold]Start reactor[/bold]. Output rises gradually. Start at 30–50% and raise it while watching the core temperature. - Higher power burns fuel faster and heats the core faster. The core only stays cool if enough gas flows through it.
## Danger Above the safe core temperature the containment field starts to fail; the hotter the core, the faster it fails. Engineering is warned over the radio as the field weakens.
If the field reaches 0%, the reactor [color=red]breaches[/color]: an explosion, a burst of superheated gas, and an electromagnetic pulse that knocks out nearby electronics. The reactor is wrecked.
[bold]Shutting down always works.[/bold] Press Shut down, keep coolant flowing, and the core cools on its own.
## Turbine Gas hotter than the turbine can take wears down its blades. A turbine with wrecked blades makes no power until it is repaired with a [color=orange]welder[/color].
